summary: The note describes the Iron Curtain as physical border defenses between western and eastern Europe, among the most heavily militarised areas in the world. It focuses on the inner German border between East and West Germany, known as die Grenze, which used double steel mesh fences in rural areas and concrete barriers like the Berlin Wall near cities. It also notes that the Berlin Wall's construction in 1961 ended the period when moving west through divided Berlin was easy.
one_line: The Iron Curtain's physical border defenses, especially the inner German border (die Grenze) and its fences and walls, and the 1961 Berlin Wall.
key_facts: The Iron Curtain took physical shape as border defenses between the countries of western and eastern Europe.
These border areas were some of the most heavily militarised areas in the world.
The so-called inner German border lay between East Germany and West Germany.
The inner German border is commonly known as die Grenze in German.
In rural areas, the inner German border was marked by double fences made of steel mesh (expanded metal) with sharp edges.
Near urban areas, a high concrete barrier similar to the Berlin Wall was built along the inner German border.
The installation of the Wall in 1961 brought an end to a decade during which the divided capital of divided Germany was one of the easiest places to move west across the Iron Curtain.
The divided capital of divided Germany was Berlin, which was one of the easiest places to cross west across the Iron Curtain before 1961.
The note states that the decade ended in 1961 with the installation of the Wall.
